title: Why Is the Sky Blue and Not Purple?

hook.text: Why is the sky blue... and not purple?

points.text: Sunlight looks white, but it is really every color of the rainbow mixed together.
When sunlight hits our atmosphere, it bumps into tiny gas molecules of nitrogen and oxygen.
Those molecules scatter short wavelengths, like blue and violet, much more than red.
This is called Rayleigh scattering, and it sends blue light bouncing all across the sky.
Violet scatters even more than blue, so why isn't the sky purple?
The Sun gives off less violet light, and our eyes are much more sensitive to blue.
At sunset, light travels through far more air, so most blue scatters away before reaching you.
That leaves the reds and oranges, which is why sunsets glow warm.

title: How Much Sleep Do You Really Need?

hook.text: Are you getting enough sleep? Most adults aren't.

points.text: Health experts say most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night.
Teenagers need even more, around 8 to 10 hours.
While you sleep, your brain sorts and stores memories from the day.
Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day helps set your body clock.
Caffeine can stay in your body for hours, so an afternoon coffee can affect your night.
Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep.
A cool, dark and quiet bedroom helps you sleep more deeply.
Ongoing poor sleep is linked to problems with mood, focus and long-term health.

sources: CDC: How Much Sleep Do I Need?

title: Octopuses Are Weirder Than You Think

hook.text: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.

points.text: Two hearts pump blood to the gills, and the third pumps it to the rest of the body.
Their blood is blue because it uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen.
About two thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, not its head.
Each arm can taste and touch what it grabs, almost like it has a mind of its own.
They can change color and skin texture in a fraction of a second to hide.
With no bones, an octopus can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak.
Octopuses in aquariums have been seen escaping their tanks and opening jars.
Most octopuses live only one to two years.

title: Why Do Leap Years Exist?

hook.text: Why does February get an extra day every four years?

points.text: A year is how long Earth takes to go around the Sun.
That trip takes about 365 days and 6 hours, not exactly 365 days.
Those extra 6 hours add up to about one full day every four years.
So we add February 29th to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.
But the real extra time is slightly less than 6 hours, so even that rule overshoots.
That's why years ending in 00 skip the leap day, unless they divide evenly by 400.
So 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not, and 2100 won't be either.
This system comes from the Gregorian calendar, introduced in 1582.

title: Do You Really Need 8 Glasses of Water a Day?

hook.text: Do you really need 8 glasses of water a day?

points.text: About 60 percent of your body is water, and you lose some every day.
But there is no single amount that is right for everyone.
How much you need depends on your size, your activity, and the weather.
Food counts too: fruit, vegetables and soups give you a good share of your water.
A simple check: pale yellow urine usually means you're drinking enough.
Thirst, headaches and tiredness can be signs you need more fluids.
You need extra water when you exercise, sweat a lot, or spend time in the heat.
Keeping a water bottle nearby is one of the easiest ways to drink more.

sources: CDC: About Water and Healthier Drinks

title: Why Honey Almost Never Goes Bad

hook.text: Honey can stay good to eat for thousands of years.

points.text: Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs.
Honey has very little water, so bacteria can't survive in it.
It is also naturally acidic, which makes it even harder for germs to grow.
Bees add an enzyme that slowly produces tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide.
If honey turns hard and cloudy, it hasn't spoiled. It has just crystallized.
Warming the jar gently in water turns it back to liquid.
A single worker bee makes only about one twelfth of a teaspoon in its whole life.
Keep the lid on tight, because honey can absorb moisture from the air.

title: How Do Airplanes Stay in the Air?

hook.text: How does a 400-ton airplane stay in the sky?

points.text: Four forces act on every plane: lift, weight, thrust and drag.
The engines create thrust, pushing the plane forward fast through the air.
As air flows over the wings, their shape and angle push air downward.
Pushing air down creates an equal push upward on the wing. That push is lift.
Air also moves faster over the curved top of the wing, which lowers the pressure there.
When lift is greater than the plane's weight, it climbs.
Pilots use flaps on the wings to create extra lift for takeoff and landing.
That's why planes need speed: no airflow over the wings means no lift.

title: What Walking Every Day Does to Your Body

hook.text: The simplest exercise there is might be the most underrated.

points.text: The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
That's just over 20 minutes a day, and brisk walking counts.
You don't have to do it all at once. Short walks add up.
Regular walking strengthens your heart and helps control blood pressure.
A short walk after a meal can help your body manage blood sugar.
Walking outdoors is also linked to better mood and less stress.
Walking with a friend makes it easier to stick with the habit.
Start where you are, and add a few minutes each week.

title: Bananas Are Berries, Strawberries Aren't

hook.text: A banana is a berry. A strawberry is not.

points.text: To botanists, a berry is a fruit that grows from one flower with one ovary.
It also has its seeds inside a soft, fleshy middle.
By that rule, bananas, grapes and kiwis are all berries.
So are tomatoes, eggplants and even avocados.
Strawberries carry their seeds on the outside, so they don't qualify.
Raspberries and blackberries aren't true berries either. They're clusters of tiny fruits.
And peanuts aren't nuts. They're legumes, like beans and peas.
Fruit names came from cooks long before scientists sorted them.

title: How Was the Great Pyramid Built?

hook.text: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years.

points.text: It was built around 4,500 years ago for the Egyptian pharaoh Khufu.
It's made of roughly 2.3 million stone blocks.
The average block weighs about two and a half tons, as much as a car.
It was likely built by thousands of paid workers, not slaves.
Archaeologists found their village nearby, with bakeries and tombs.
Workers probably dragged blocks on sledges and wet the sand to reduce friction.
Ramps were used to move the stones up as the pyramid grew.
It was first about 146 meters tall, and its sides line up closely with north, south, east and west.

title: The 20-20-20 Rule for Tired Eyes

hook.text: Staring at screens all day? Try the 20-20-20 rule.

points.text: Every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away, or 6 meters.
Keep looking for 20 seconds. That's the whole rule.
It gives the focusing muscles in your eyes a short break.
We blink less when we look at screens, which can leave eyes dry.
Blinking on purpose a few times helps keep your eyes moist.
Keep your screen about an arm's length away, slightly below eye level.
Match screen brightness to the room to reduce glare.
If your eyes still hurt or your vision changes, see an eye doctor.

sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology: Computers, Digital Devices and Eye Strain

title: The Strangest Ways Animals Sleep

hook.text: Some animals sleep with half their brain awake.

points.text: Dolphins rest one half of their brain at a time so they can keep breathing.
Sea otters often hold paws while sleeping so they don't drift apart.
Some seabirds, called frigatebirds, can sleep in short bursts while flying.
Giraffes in the wild sleep only a few hours a day, often in tiny naps.
Koalas sleep up to 18 to 22 hours a day to save energy.
Horses can doze standing up, thanks to a special locking system in their legs.
Sperm whales take short naps floating upright in the water.
And cats sleep around 12 to 16 hours a day.

title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?

hook.text: Rivers are fresh water. So why is the ocean salty?

points.text: Rain is slightly acidic, and over time it wears down rocks on land.
That releases minerals and salts, which rivers carry to the sea.
When sun heats the ocean, water evaporates but the salt stays behind.
Over millions of years, that salt has built up.
Vents and volcanoes on the seafloor add even more minerals.
On average, ocean water is about 3.5 percent salt.
The Dead Sea is almost ten times saltier, which is why people float so easily in it.
Most of the salt in the sea is the same kind you put on food: sodium chloride.

title: You're Probably Washing Your Hands Too Fast

hook.text: Studies find many people wash their hands for only a few seconds.

points.text: Health experts recommend scrubbing with soap for at least 20 seconds.
That's about as long as humming 'Happy Birthday' twice.
Soap works by breaking apart the oily layer that surrounds many germs.
Don't forget the backs of your hands, between your fingers, and under your nails.
Rinse well under clean running water.
Dry your hands fully, because germs spread more easily from wet hands.
Wash before eating, after the bathroom, and after coughing or sneezing.
No sink? Use a hand sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol.

sources: CDC: When and How to Wash Your Hands

title: Space Facts That Sound Fake But Aren't

hook.text: A day on Venus is longer than its year.

points.text: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only 225 to orbit the Sun.
Astronauts' footprints on the Moon could last millions of years, because there's no wind.
Astronauts get a few centimeters taller in space, as their spines stretch out.
The space station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
So its crew can see around 16 sunrises every day.
Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a giant enough bathtub.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, so you always see the Sun as it was.
There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.

title: The Internet Lives at the Bottom of the Ocean

hook.text: Your internet probably crosses the ocean floor.

points.text: Almost all data between continents travels through cables on the seabed, not satellites.
Together, these cables stretch well over a million kilometers.
Inside are thin glass fibers that carry data as pulses of light.
In the deep ocean, many cables are only about as thick as a garden hose.
Near the shore they get thicker armor to protect them from anchors and fishing gear.
When a cable breaks, special repair ships haul it up and fix it at sea.
The first cable across the Atlantic carried telegraph messages back in 1858.
So the next time you send a message abroad, it may be racing along the seafloor.

title: Sunscreen Mistakes Almost Everyone Makes

hook.text: You can get sunburned on a cloudy day.

points.text: Up to 80 percent of the Sun's UV rays can pass through clouds.
Dermatologists recommend a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher.
Most people use too little. Adults need about a shot glass worth for the whole body.
Reapply every two hours, and after swimming or sweating.
Don't forget your ears, neck, feet and the back of your hands.
UV rays are usually strongest from about 10 in the morning to 4 in the afternoon.
Water, sand and snow reflect sunlight, adding to your exposure.
A hat and UV-blocking sunglasses protect the spots sunscreen misses.

sources: American Academy of Dermatology: How to apply sunscreen

title: Weird Facts About Your Own Body

hook.text: You were born with about 300 bones. Now you have 206.

points.text: As babies grow, many of their bones fuse together.
Your stomach lining replaces itself every few days so acid doesn't digest it.
The human body gives off a very faint light, but it's far too weak for our eyes to see.
Your nose can tell apart a huge number of different smells.
You're slightly taller in the morning than at night.
During the day, the discs in your spine get squeezed. They recover while you sleep.
Your fingerprints are unique, even if you're an identical twin.
And your heart beats around 100,000 times every day.

title: Why Do We Have Time Zones?

hook.text: Before time zones, every town set its own clock.

points.text: Towns used to set noon by when the Sun was highest in their own sky.
That meant two nearby towns could be several minutes apart.
Railroads made this a real problem: train timetables were a mess.
In 1883, North American railroads adopted standard time zones.
In 1884, countries agreed to measure longitude from Greenwich, in London.
Earth spins 15 degrees every hour, so each standard zone is roughly 15 degrees wide.
But borders bend the lines: China uses one time zone across the whole country.
Some places are half an hour off, like India, and Nepal is 45 minutes off.

title: The Nutrient Most People Don't Eat Enough Of

hook.text: Most people eat only about half the fiber they need.

points.text: Fiber is the part of plant food your body can't fully digest.
It helps keep digestion regular and helps you feel full longer.
US guidelines suggest about 25 grams a day for women and 38 for men.
Beans, lentils and peas are some of the richest sources.
Whole grains like oats and brown rice beat white bread and white rice.
Fruit and vegetables count too, especially with the skin on.
Nuts and seeds make easy high-fiber snacks.
Add fiber slowly and drink enough water, to avoid bloating.

sources: Dietary Guidelines for Americans; Institute of Medicine fiber recommendations

title: Things Your Cat and Dog Won't Tell You

hook.text: Your cat can't taste anything sweet.

points.text: Cats lack a working sweet taste receptor, so sugar means nothing to them.
Every dog's nose print is unique, like a human fingerprint.
Dogs' sense of smell is thousands of times stronger than ours.
Cats usually only meow at people, not at other adult cats.
Many dogs can learn the names of dozens of words and objects.
Cats spend around 12 to 16 hours a day asleep.
A dog's wagging tail doesn't always mean it's happy. Watch the whole body.
And when a cat slowly blinks at you, it's a sign it trusts you.

title: Black Holes Explained in 90 Seconds

hook.text: There's a place in space where even light can't escape.

points.text: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong nothing can get out.
Many form when a huge star runs out of fuel and collapses on itself.
The edge you can't come back from is called the event horizon.
Near a black hole, time runs slower than it does far away.
We can't see black holes directly, but we see the glowing gas swirling around them.
In 2019, scientists released the first image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.
There's one at the center of our own galaxy called Sagittarius A*.
It's about 4 million times the mass of our Sun.

title: A 60-Second Breathing Trick to Calm Down

hook.text: Feeling stressed? Your breath can help in about a minute.

points.text: When you're stressed, your breathing often gets fast and shallow.
Slow, steady breathing can help your body shift toward a calmer state.
Try box breathing: breathe in slowly for a count of four.
Hold your breath gently for four.
Breathe out slowly for four, then hold again for four.
Repeat for one to two minutes, keeping your shoulders relaxed.
Making your out-breath longer than your in-breath can also help you relax.
If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally.

sources: Harvard Health Publishing: Relaxation techniques: Breath control helps quell errant stress response

title: History Timelines That Will Break Your Brain

hook.text: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

points.text: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC.
Cleopatra lived around 30 BC, about 2,500 years later.
The Moon landing was in 1969, about 2,000 years after her.
Oxford University was already teaching students before the Aztec capital was founded in 1325.
Woolly mammoths still lived on a remote Arctic island when the pyramids were being built.
Nintendo was founded in 1889, and it started by making playing cards.
The fax machine was invented in the 1840s, before the telephone.
History is a lot more overlapped than school timelines make it look.

title: How Lightning Actually Works

hook.text: A bolt of lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.

points.text: Inside storm clouds, ice crystals and soft hail crash into each other.
Those collisions separate electric charges inside the cloud.
When the charge gets big enough, it jumps as a giant spark: lightning.
A bolt can heat the air to around 30,000 degrees Celsius.
That's about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
The air expands so fast it makes a boom. That's thunder.
Count the seconds between flash and thunder, and divide by three, for the distance in kilometers.
If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck. Go indoors.

title: How Much Sugar Is Too Much?

hook.text: One can of soda can have more sugar than you should eat in a whole day.

points.text: The World Health Organization says added sugars should be under 10 percent of daily calories.
It suggests that cutting to under 5 percent brings extra benefits.
For most adults, 5 percent is about 25 grams, or 6 teaspoons, a day.
A regular 330 ml can of cola has around 35 grams of sugar.
Sugar hides in sauces, cereals, flavored yogurts and breads.
Check labels for words like syrup, dextrose, sucrose and fructose.
The sugar naturally found in whole fruit and plain milk doesn't count toward that limit.
Swapping one sugary drink a day for water is an easy place to start.

sources: WHO guideline: Sugars intake for adults and children

title: Food Facts You Won't Believe

hook.text: Carrots weren't always orange.

points.text: Early carrots were mostly purple or yellow.
Orange carrots became popular thanks to Dutch growers in the 1600s.
In the 1830s, ketchup was sold in America as a medicine in pill form.
Ancient Mesoamericans used cacao beans as money.
And chocolate was a bitter drink for centuries before it became a candy bar.
A pineapple can take up to two years to grow, and each plant makes one fruit at a time.
Cashews grow hanging from the bottom of a fruit called the cashew apple.
And sliced bread was only sold commercially starting in 1928.

title: The Stone That Cracked Egyptian Hieroglyphs

hook.text: For centuries, no one could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. Then one stone changed that.

points.text: In 1799, French soldiers in Egypt found a broken stone slab near the town of Rashid, or Rosetta.
It carried a decree from 196 BC, written in three scripts.
The top was in hieroglyphs, the middle in Demotic, and the bottom in ancient Greek.
Scholars could already read Greek, so they had a key to the other two.
Names of rulers were circled in hieroglyphs, which gave important clues.
In 1822, Jean-François Champollion announced he had cracked the code.
His work unlocked thousands of years of Egyptian history.
Today the Rosetta Stone is one of the most visited objects in the British Museum.

title: Sitting All Day? Do This Every Hour

hook.text: If you sit most of the day, your body needs a reminder to move.

points.text: Long periods of sitting are linked to higher risks for heart disease and diabetes.
The WHO advises adults to limit sitting and break it up with activity.
Try standing up and moving for a few minutes every 30 to 60 minutes.
Take phone calls standing, or walk while you talk.
Use the stairs instead of the elevator when you can.
Stretch your neck, shoulders and hips to ease stiffness.
Set a timer or a phone reminder until moving becomes a habit.
Small breaks add up across a whole week.

title: The Ocean Is Stranger Than Space

hook.text: We have better maps of Mars than of our own ocean floor.

points.text: Only about a quarter of the seafloor has been mapped in high detail.
The deepest point, the Challenger Deep, is about 11 kilometers down.
If you dropped Mount Everest in there, its peak would still be underwater.
Tiny ocean plants called phytoplankton make a large share of the oxygen we breathe.
A blue whale's heart weighs around 180 kilograms.
Some deep-sea creatures make their own light, called bioluminescence.
The ocean holds about 97 percent of Earth's water.
Scientists think most ocean species haven't even been discovered yet.
